maintopic: CIVIL SERVICE ACT, 1918, AMENDMENT EMPLOYEES-REVENUE AND CITY POST OFFICES
speechtext: I am sure we all welcome this legislation if for no other purpose than to introduce the Postmaster General (Mr. Murphy) to the House of Commons for this session. He differs very strikingly from his colleague the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) in that he is not pestering the House with chicken-feed legislation every other day. Perhaps though he will signalize the occasion by one of his usual illuminating explanations of this bill.

maintopic: CIVIL SERVICE ACT, 1918, AMENDMENT EMPLOYEES-REVENUE AND CITY POST OFFICES
speechtext:
I thank my right hon. friend for his introduction, but if he had been in his seat the other day when this matter came up on resolution he would have heard the explanation. It is very simple. There was a section in the Post Office Act, which was in force up till 1918, providing the method for changing revenue post offices into city post offices. In that year the act was consolidated, and, for some reason I have not been able to ascertain but apparently through oversight, this particular section was omitted. The present bill is to re-enact that section, and the explanatory note says:
The abject of this bill is to enable the Civil Service Commission to appoint experienced employees of postmasters of offices paid by percentage on revenue, when the status of such offices is changed to the staff basis. It will, for all practical purposes, be a re-enactment of

Supply-Marine and Fisheries
section twelve of chapter eight of the Statutes of 1910, but modified in such a way as to make the procedure regarding appointments to the civil service, conform to the procedure at present in effect, that is, on certificate of the Civil Service Commission.

maintopic: CIVIL SERVICE ACT, 1918, AMENDMENT EMPLOYEES-REVENUE AND CITY POST OFFICES
speechtext: There is an amalgamated body of civil servants which comprises a branch consisting of postal workers, and I know the minister will agree that generally speaking they seem to be very reasonable men. I have found them very reasonable at any rate, and I think they are interested in this legislation. Would the Postmaster General mind stating if any conference has been held in regard to this matter with representatives of this body?

maintopic: CIVIL SERVICE ACT, 1918, AMENDMENT EMPLOYEES-REVENUE AND CITY POST OFFICES
speechtext:
I may say that conferences have been held with representatives of that body, and my information is that there is no objection whatever to the proposed legislation.
Subsection (a) agreed to.
On subsection (b)-Salary.

maintopic: CIVIL SERVICE ACT, 1918, AMENDMENT EMPLOYEES-REVENUE AND CITY POST OFFICES
speechtext: When this matter was before the House on the introduction of the resolution on which the present bill is founded, the minister was kind enough to give an explanation with respect to bringing in so-called revenue offices. At that time I, and a number of other members also, pointed out to him the desirability of having certain of the larger revenue offices included in the category known as staff offices. I should like to ask him now if the government intend to take any action on the line indicated, or do they propose to adhere to the limitation which he then stated?-that 'is in the case of towns of a population of 10,000 or over and a minimum revenue of $35,000 or over. I feel that the limitation is too high and that there should be a reduction; also that in certain of the large towns where the revenues are large the employees of those post offices should be brought in under the Civil Service Act.

speechtext:

The House in committee of Supply, Mr. Gordon in the chair.
Fisheries-building fishways and clearing rivers, *30,000.

How much was spent
last year?

speakeroldname: Hon. P. J. A. CARDIN (Minister of Marine and Fisheries):
speechtext: Spent last year-$7,690.

In view of that fact, why
does the minister want $30,000 this year?

It is quite impossible to
foretell what the expenses will be, because this item provides for the removing of obstructions to fish ascending rivers and streams to their spawning areas, and the building of fishways in dams across such rivers and streams. Particularly in British Columbia rivers, log jams are continually forming along those rivers and often become so complete that the ascending fish are unable to get beyond. Also natural obstructions are sometimes encountered in streams and rivers. In 1923-24 a sum of $20,316 was spent for this purpose.

Why does the minister
say "particularly in British Columbia"?
Conditions in that province, on account of the mountains, are more difficult than in other provinces.

Is there any money spent
in any other province, or is it all spent in British Columbia?
The department is spending money in all the other provinces; this item covers the whole country.

Is not the reason why so much expenditure is necessary in British Columbia the fact that the salmon runs up the various rivers, and it is necessary, in order to preserve that tremendous industry, that the salmon shall get to their spawning ground?
Exactly.

With reference to the new fishway and dam at Maysville on the Nash-waak river: some two or three years ago a large dam was built by the Nashwaak Pulp and Paper Company at this point, and a fishway was installed, which for some wholly unaccountable reason was put in the wrong place, so that when the water went down the foot of the fishway was out of the water below, and the salmon, which formerly used

Supply-Marine and Fisheries
that river in very large numbers, and which would again use it if there were an adequate fishway, were unable to get through. Has a new fishway been installed, at whose expense, and is it now functioning properly?

A new concrete fishway
was built to replace the former one. The department has paid one-half of the cost, the total being $513.

Who paid the cost of the
original fishway?
The company.

Why should not the company pay all the cost of the new fishway? I understand they were very insistent on the location of the old fishway, which proved to be an error, and I see no reason why the company should not pay all the cost of the new one, which is not so excessive.

I am informed that the
act provides that when the fishway has to be replaced the department is to pay half of the cost.

It is a matter of the
statute.
Yes.
Is the new fishway functioning properly? It is a very important matter.

The department will be
able to ascertain that during the coming season.

When was the new
fishway installed?
It was completed last fall, but, I am told, too late to find out if it would operate properly.

It may seem rather a small matter, but I wish to mention the state of affairs that exists on the small streams in the prairie provinces. The Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian National Railway have built dams across the streams. The fishways are put out and the fish cannot get through them whenever the water gets a little low. I brought the matter up during two sessions, and the reply was that the fishways were built according to instructions. It seems rather strange. These fishways may be built according to regulations, but the fish do not seem to understand it, because they cannot get up the fishways.
They should be instructed.

It seems to be a small thing, *but you must take into consideration conditions on the prairies, where the game fish, more particularly down in the southern parts, are very rare in the stream. There are lots of pike. To the people who are in the habit of catching salmon and other game fish pike seem rather a poor affair, but then they are very much prized in the prairie provinces, and I know that hundreds of thousands of them are destroyed at the foot of the fishways. I hope the minister will look into the situation at Pipestone, and the White Mud River. We have two fishways on the Pipestone, one on the Canadian National and one on the Canadian Pacific, and every year when the fish begin to run they die by the thousands. It is a very serious matter for people living along the banks of the stream.
I have a note that repairs were made to fishways in the dams at Gladstone and Westbourne. Both were inspected at the time when fish were ascending and the latter found to be effective.
This is on the Pipestone. It is a very important stream.

That is at White Mud
River.

In reference to the item
of clearing of rivers, how much was spent in the province of New Brunswick last year, what rivers were cleared, and what methods were adopted? How was the work done? Was it done by day's work under the department, or let out by contract?

I have a note here which
reads:
New Brunswick, construction of fishways, Marysville fishway, York county, $513.13.
I am informed there was no difficulty in New Brunswick. The money was spent for the building of fishways, and there was no obstruction.

The minister means the
officers of the department did not look for any obstruction. Under this heading of clearing of rivers it has been customary to take out the logs and snags in the river St. John below Fredericton, when there is navigation. For many years this work was performed by a company operating on the river. Last year I was informed, this work had been performed by the department with the crew and necessary boats. I think that was a very poor policy to adont, because it involved certain capital expenditure, and the boats of the department could not be used elsewhere. That

Supply-Marine and Fisheries
sort of equipment could not be used for anything else. It may have been two years ago that I mentioned the matter.
I should like to point out to the minister that in the portion of the river below Fredericton, called the Orom-oeto shoals, which is silted in every year in my memory, and which have not been dredged since the war, there are numerous snags and sunken logs, and this constitutes a menace to navigation, and in the months of July and August there is need for this work to go on. I think the minister should give instructions to have the work examined by engineers of the department. I believe the river is under an engineer of the Public Works dparbment. I am not at all sure if it is under the minister's department. Personally, I do not see why the question of clearing rivers should not 'be under the Public Works department instead of under the Marine and Fisheries; but that is immaterial so long as I have assurance that some attention will be given by the administration to the situation. Every year there are more or less sunken logs on the shoal parts of the St. John river. These logs become water-logged; they sink and, as a rule, they are a danger to navigation of small steamers that ply upon the river. It is necessary that something be done. Has the department a report made last year as to the condi: ion of the river, or was the matter looked into at all.

My information is that this work would come under the Public Works department. My department is only looking after small rivers or non-navigable waters. The great work of clearing navigable waters is under the control of the Public Works department. .

I take this opportunity
of urging upon the department the importance o.f care and oversight of the fishways and of clearing the rivers. I have on several occasions drawn the attention of the department to a very considerable number of rivers which suffer materially from obstructions. I rather gather from what the minister said that in New Brunswick no considerable number of rivers had been drawn to his attention as regards obstructions. Acute observers, men familiar with localities, assure me that the propagation, more especially of salmon, is greatly hindered by obstructions in a large number of rivers. The files of his department will show, I would think, probably ten or twelve rivers, given specifically by name, in which those conditions obtain. From what information I have been able to gather, I think the department is in-249
dined to deal with this matter more especially this year, so that I believe the difficulties in some of the streams will be met. Necessarily there must be some relationship between hatcheries and mechanical obstructions in streams, and it is necessary to deal with both of those. But without the experience and knowledge of lan expert, I believe a proportionate expenditure and care should lean in the direction of removal of obstructions in rivers rather than towards hatcheries, because it is the natural propagation that we must more particularly look after. It is my firm conviction that in any case in New Brunswick if the fish have a fair opportunity of going up the streams and ordinary protective care is carried out, the need of hatcheries will be greatly lessened. I can assure the minister that at the present time it is the opinion of sportsmen and men who are familiar with the area, that the great loss of fish is due to obstructions in the streams. I feel confident the names of many of these rivers are now in the department and I think the department is disposed to attend to the matter. But, speaking as a general proposition, I believe the number of fish depends more especially on the opportunity to get up a river to spawn rather than on the artificial method of hatcheries.

What rivers in
Nova Scotia have been dealt with in regard to obstructions?

Removal of obstructions in Nova Scotia has taken place on the Salmon river-Porter stream, Halifax county; Meadows brook, Cape Breton county; Beaver-dam brook, Queen's county; Curry's brook, Cape Breton county; Grass Cove pond, Victoria county; Ferguson's brook, Cape Breton county; St. Joseph de Moine, Inverness county; Murphy's lake, King's county; Black brook, Cape Breton county. Fishways were constructed on the Mersey river, Queen's county, Potanoc river, Queen's county; Grand river, Richmond County; Mushamush river, Lunenburg county; River Phillip, Lunenburg county; East river, Lunenburg county; Pictaux river, Annapolis county.

I am glad, indeed, to hear such a comprehensive list of rivers that have been dealt with, and I trust that others will be attended to during the coming season. In my experience, I can name places where the spawning beds have been partically destroyed by the accumulation of logs, roots and rubbish. It is a well known fact that salmon in particular do not frequent the rivers in which those conditions exist.



Supply-Marine and Fisheries
As so much attention has been paid to the natural breeding of fish, it is important that all these pools and gravel beds should be kept free of rubbish so that the fish may spawn in those parts of the rivers. Whilst the department has apparently made efforts-I do not think I can say strenuous efforts-to carry out the protective system in order to guard the rivers sufficiently, I tlhink it has fallen very far short of its duty in that respect. I know that a great deal of poaching and other illegal work is going on in the rivers of Nova Scotia. Occasionally arrests have been made, but I am not able to recall that any convictions have been brought about. There are places where, under the eyes of the guardians, wrongdoing is constantly being carried out and, in my judgment and I think in the judgment of most of those who in former years used to frequent the rivers of Nova Scotia for sport, salmon fishing will soon be a thing of the past. The rivers are getting into such a condition that it is not worth the sportsman's while to visit them. Some of our best streams, such as the Gold and Tangier rivers and others 1 could name, are not to-day visited by those who are seeking sport in the hope of being in any degree successful. I would call the minister's attention particularly to this question of protection and ask him whether some more vigorous policy could not be pursued than that which has so far been in force.

The minister is still following the old, wornout practice of appointing political guardians; for that is what they are in New Brunswick. The guardians there are the local heelers who are appointed without regard to any consideration of fitness; so long as they can paddle a canoe they are evidently considered fit to be guardians. This government is only following what has been the practice for generations; but it is a wornout practice. The very fact that these men are political appointees robs them of any power they might have. A guardian to be successful must be fearless and courageous, and he cannot be either fearless or courageous if he has to think of the voters. So far as the St. John river is concerned, there are altogether too few guardians, notwithstanding that this is the largest river in New Brunswick, where the propagation of the bay of Fundy salmon takes place. On a stretch of seventy-five miles between York and Sunbury I doubt whether there are more than three or four guardians altogether. These men cannot possibly prevent poaching, and they are not the right type to do it when they are appointed.

I do not know very much about the rivers on the mainland of Nova Scotia, but I do know something about the best salmon fishing river in all the Maritime provinces; I refer to the Margaree. My hon. friend (Mr. Doueet) knows the Margaree very well; he was born in that vicinity. In the last eight years or so there has been an annual increase in the number of sportsmen who go to the Margaree, and I have myself visited that stream quite often, it being in my native home, although I do not represent that county. I go up the river every Saturday and have a very enjoyable time fishing; I do not fish on Sunday. Last year six new bunga'ows were built along the river to take care of the increasing tourist traffic and they were inadequate to provide the needed accommodation. Some three weeks ago I happened to be down there on a visit and I discovered that this year the bungalow accommodation had been increased to ten new houses. The river is well taken care of. We have in that part of the country what is known as the Cape Breton Fishing and Sports Association and in nine cases out of ten the members of this body are non-partisan; the association comprises both Liberals and Conservatives with, I presume, a few Labour and Farmer representatives thrown in. And very often their requests for capable guardians are favourably considered by the department and those whom they recommend are appointed. In Mr. A. G. McLeod, the inspector of fisheries for Cape Breton, we have a very splendid official. I may tell my hon. friend (Mr. Hanson) that this gentleman is an appointee of the old government, having been selected before the Civil Service Commission came in; but, notwithstanding that fact and the fact that all his affiliations are Conservative, I want to say in his behalf that he is perhaps the best inspector we have ever had in Cape Breton. Under him are four or five, probably six, overseers appointed by the Civil Service Commission, who of course are all non-partisan; they are mostly returned soldiers. So far as I am aware these men are all doing efficient work.

Are these overseers the
actual guardians?
No.
That is the point.

But they also do the
work of guardians. The guardians however are under them and no man who is not favourably known to these overseers is appointed. I have practical experience in my

Supply-Marine and Fisheries
own county as well as in the county of Inverness through which the Margaree runs. I know something also of St. Mary river in Guysborough county, and for some reason which I am unable to understand that river has been going down as a resort for tourists *interested in salmon fishing. However, I want to give the officials of the department, not particularly the minister, but those under him, and especially the official gentleman who is at present on the floor of the House, credit for what has been done in this matter. 1 desire to pay them this compliment, that so far as the island of Cape Breton is concerned at any rate-and we think that the very best salmon and trout fishing is to be enjoyed there-we are getting the best protection possible. As a matter of fact, besides American tourists, we have very frequent visitors from the provinces of Ontario and Quebec who go there season after season and lend the guardians a helping hand in protecting the salmon streams from poachers and others who make an illicit use of them. As to the remarks of my hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. Black), I do not know anything about the peninsula of Nova Scotia, but I have some knowledge of the St. Mary river where I go occasionally. I have something else to say on this subject but my remarks will be more pertinent to item Fish Culture.
Will the minister kindly give us a detailed statement, similar to the one he made for the province of Nova Scotia, showing what work has been done in New Brunswick.

The department did not remove any obstructions in the New Brunswick *rivers, but it has built a fishway at Marysville, in York county. Perhaps I had better read the memorandum I have on this matter:
Marysville fishway, York county, $5X3.13. A new concrete fishway was built replacing one previously built by the company which had proved ineffective. The department paid one-half the cost of the new fishway which amounted to the above figure.
Robertson lake, St. John county, $78.37. New partitions were placed in the fishway to replace the old ones which were ineffective and in need of extensive repairs.
Salmon river, Victoria county, $422.90. The department paid one-half the cost of a fishway in a dam owned by Mr. Joseph Cote. The latter had not been required to build the fishway when he built his dam, and claimed this exemption because of the fact that prices were now much higher than when he built and, as a consequence the fishway would cost much more.
Theriault fishway, Victoria county, $27.75. An extension was built at the foot of the fishway to improve conditions for the asCent of salmon.
Is there any list of rivers cleared?

No clearing was done in New Brunswick last year.
249J

I hope next year the
minister will give me more encouragement.
It is the department's intention to send an engineer to the Maritime provinces to carry on an investigation, and it purposes to undertake any work that may be recommended by him.

The most important salmon river we have in Canada is the Restigouche river, which is the boundary between New Brunswick and Quebec. Does the department still exercise its activities in connection with the sailmon rivers of Quebec, or has it transferred its control entirely to the provincial government?

Our control in the fisheries
of Quebec has been handed over to the provincial authorities.

Including
the clearing of the rivers?

Everything.
Mr. MARjCIL (Bonaventure): What about the Restigouche, an intenprovineial river?

The Quebec side is under the control of the provincial government.
Mr. MARjCIL (Bonaventure):	Was any
work done on the rivers last year?

I am informed they are
(Hear.
Was there ever in existence a regulation to prevent sport fishing on rivers or streams on Sundays? If so, is such regulation still in effect in Nova Scotia?
There is nothing to prevent Sunday fishing in Nova Scotia.
Has the department been investigating the possibility of installing a fishway at the mouitfa of the Magaguadavie river? And what are the prospects of converting it into a salmon river?
Nothing has been done up to the present, but our engineer is going down there this summer to make another investigation. The result of his investigation last year was not satisfactory.

Then the department has not abandoned the idea of putting a fishway at that point? This river is controlled by an American company which makes ground wood pulp at that point. While it is a somewhat important industry, yet I think it should not be allowed to prevent the in-4 pm. stallation of a fishway if iin the opinion of the officials of the department such a fishway would be effective. I

Supply-Marine and Fisheries
would not wanit to insist upon its installation unless the department had some reasonable assurance that it would function; but if the department arrives at that conclusion, I think it should act notwithstanding the opposition which will no doubt emanate from the St. George Pulp & Paper Company.
As I said, we are (making a full investigation and will act on the engineer's report.

Has the department ever taken into consideration the advisability of making Sunday a close time in order'that the fish might be able to get to their spawning grounds? I think such a regulation would aid the fisheries generally, apart from the moral standpoint altogether. I think more harm is done to our fisheries by Sunday fueling than by all other fishing throughout the week. People go off early in the morning in hundreds, and whip practically every stream. They are also the cause of setting fires. Moreover, there is a day set aside for rest-the seventh day.

Saturday.
Mr. MARTELiL: You can take it scripturally or in any other way, but one day in seven is necessary for man physically as well as morally. If the department does not act from the high moral standpoint, I submit that it should from the standpoint of the protection of our fisheries. In British Columbia there is a dose time in order that the salmon may ascend to their spawning grounds. There is the same necessity for such a regulation in Nova Scotia, and I think Sunday should be declared a close day for our fish. I am confident that a regulation of this kind would meet with the approval of practically everybody save those who want to desecrate the Sabbath and who do not care what happens to tlhe fish.

In Nova Scotia there is
a regulation preventing fishing with nets on Sundays, but there is no restriction in regard to sport fishing.

There should be. Will
the minister take that into consideration?

I thoroughly agree with the principle enunciated by the member for Hants. I know that many communities throughout Nova Scotia were very much annoyed when Sunday fishing became permissible, and it is the wish of those people not to be disturbed by those who thresh the river on Sundays and in other ways annoy the residents. I think in the interests of the

fisheries it is only right that on Sundays the fish should have an opportunity of moving up river from pool to pool without being disturbed.

Mr. Chairman, I agree
with what these two hon. gentlemen (Mr. Martell and Mr. Black) say about Sunday fishing from the point of view of the fish; but I do not see any more harm in Sunday fishing than in Sunday golf, Sunday motoring, Sunday card playing and a dozen other forms of recreation that our people indulge in. Fishing is a good, healthful recreation; and if golfing is not harmful neither is fishing.

Golfing is indulged in
in private places.

Why do in secret what
you would not care to practise in public?
I do not believe in that sort of thing. I think we will have to leave the matter to the conscience of the individual.

I thoroughly agree that
a regulation prohibiting Sunday fishing would not only be good for the fish but .also would be good for the community. The analogy drawn by my hon. friend from York-Bunbury (Mr. Hanson) between Sunday fishing and Sunday golf is not a good one. If you play golf you do not disturb anyone, for you play the game on private grounds, but I do not think it is proper that hundreds of people should fish our rivers from early Sunday morning till late at night and incidentally disturb the local residents. I heartily agree with my hon. friends from Hants and Halifax that the department should take seriously into consideration the advisability of making a regulation under the act to stop Sunday fishing. This would give the fish an opportunity to get to their spawning grounds and would avoid a great deal of annoyance to those living along the rivers. Alewife fishing is prohibited from sundown on Saturday afternoon until nine o'clock Monday morning.
That is commercial fishing?

Yes. There is no doubt
it was the intention to give the alewives an opportunity of getting into the lakes to spawn.
A similar restriction would give our salmon and trout an equal opportunity. I would ask the minister and the officials of his department to take seriously into consideration the remarks of my hon. friends from Hants and Halifax in this regard.

Supply-Marine and Fisheries

Mr. Chairman, I hope if
the suggestion made by the hon. members who have just spoken is to take effect it will be restricted to Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. They seem to have got away from the item under discussion which, I understand, is fish ladders, and I do not quite see what bearing this discussion has on those things. It seems to have developed into a funny mixture of morality and supposed fish preservation. Is the idea to prevent people sinning by fishing on Sunday, or is it to benefit the fish?-because we have had the two subjects so mixed up that it is difficult to decide what is really desired. If it is wrong to fish on Sunday, that has nothing to do with this subject, and this is not an appropriate item under which to bring that up.
Wihat are we discussing?
We are discussing the -c'earing out of rivers and fish ladders.
Jacob's ladder.

This is not Jacob's ladder we are discussing, but the clearing out of streams. I entirely agree with the remarks of the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) that this is not the place and this is not the way to legislate men into changing their dhurch-going or religious points of view. That is entirely a matter for everyone's own personal conscience.
A great deal has been said about the disturbance caused by these fishers. I never knew before that fishers were a noisy and boisterous people, I had always thought their occupation required them to be quiet, and raise no noise at all. Another suggestion was made from the other side of the House that they started fires. Do they start .more fires on Sunday than on Saturday? That is not logical. The suggestion is also made that they thresh the rivers and streams. But that does not make much noise. The suggestion is that it annoys the residents in the locality. It will not annoy them if they also are not on that stream themselves on Sunday, will it? Is not a great deal of the trouble just a little bit of selfishness? These people object to the worker who works six days a week, coming out on his one free day and getting his share of the fish, which, after all, are not the exclusive property of the local people. Cannot a great deal of this trouble be traced to a little hoggishness on the part of the country dwellers who know that if the worker can be forbidden fishing on Sunday, he will likely
not fish at all and leave more sport for them?
I am a country dweller myself, but we must let the man from the city or village get a chance of health and fresh air and innocent recreation on Sunday. However, I am prepared to allow these peculiar ideas of the previous speakers to be carried out in New Brunswick and Nova Scotia as long as they are not applied to the Province of British Columbia and we in that province are allowed freedom of conscience and liberty of action.

I am surprised that a member from Nova Scotia should tell the country that there is so much fishing going on in his province on Sunday. In our section, in New Brunswick, the Sabbath is observed much better than that. However, that is apart from the vote under discussion.
I rise to suggest this to the minister: If the department undertakes the clearing of rivers in New Brunswick, some attention should be paid to the Richibuoto and its tributaries, the Bass, the St. Nicholas, and the Moulie's; and other rivers such as the Cocagne, the Buc-touche, the Kouehibouguac, and others. These are all great rivers for the propagation of fish, but I understand that a number of mill dams have been constructed on them, with no proper fishways, and consequently the fish cannot get up the streams to spawn. This is very important, and I submit that the officials of the department should see that proper accommodation is provided so that the fish can get up these streams, and thus aid in the development of this great industry on these rivers.

Would the minister explain what this is for?

The proposed appropriation is to enable investigation to be made into the best method of preparing fish for market; also the dissemination of useful and important information among the fishermen and dealers; also to enable measures to be taken for the expansion of the demand for fish, and to carry out undertakings of importance for the benefit of the fisheries the necessity for which may arise from time to time and would not otherwise be provided for. Under this appropriation educational stations are being established at Halifax and Prince Rupert. Assistance is also being given to the Canadian Fisheries' Association in carrying on an advertising campaign looking to the expansion of the trade.

In connection, with the
conservation of deep-sea fisheries I want to remind the minister that during the last session, of this parliament the Marine and Fisheries committee adopted unanimously a resolution moved by the hon. member for Prince (Mr. . MacLean) that, owing to the extremely rough weather in the month of October practically every year, the open season for lobsters, which to-day is from the 16th of August to the 15th of October, should be changed to read from the 6th of August to the 5th of October. That resolution, as I say, was passed unanimously on the 17th of June, and it was communicated by the clerk of the committee on the 16th of July to the Deputy Minister of Marine and Fisheries. That was in accord with and following a suggestion made at a meeting of that same committee held on the 30th day of April, 1924, at which meeting it was stated that an expert of the department was expected to visit the Maritime provinces and study the various phases of the fisheries in those provinces. Now the claim is made by some, possibly by some departmental official that the fish would not be in a condition to place on the market so early in August. The bulk of the fishermen contend otherwise. As a matter of fact, in the month of February last year a delegate from that section,, and representing practically all the fishermen of the section, came to Ottawa with -a petition asking that the open season should run from the 1st day of August instead of the 16th. We in the Marine and Fisheries committee thought that we would make a compromise, and we suggested advancing it by ten days for last year only, particularly in view of the fact that an official of the department would be on the ground and would be able to get first-hand knowledge as to whether the fish were really in a condition for market so early in the month of August. Unfortunately that was not done. There is no use harping on that, but what I do say is this: I understand that Dr. Knight of the Biological Board is to spend some time in the Maritime provinces this summer in connection with the deep-sea fisheries and with the canning establishments, and I humbly suggest to the minister, through you, Mr. Chairman, that the fishermen of that section of the country from Choekfish to Bale Verte, be given the privilege of fishing for lobsters beginning on the 6th day of August and running to the 5th day of October, following the suggestion that was made by the Marine and Fisheries committee last year, and Dr. Knight would then have an opportunity to learn whether the 
lobsters at that time of the month were in a condition to be marketed.
Now, Mr. Chairman, it is well known to all those who reside on the straits of Northumberland that practically every year, during the firsit two weeks of October, severe storms occur which occasion great damage to the fishing gear of the men engaged in this industry. As a matter of fact the fishermen are anxious to bring their gear ashore during the first week of that month, rather than expose it to the risk of being completely destroyed by the storms which make their appearance almost every year. If the lobsters are fit for the market at the time referred to why not allow the fishermen to take them, and in that way enable them to obtain a better livelihood than they have been able to secure in the past? I make the suggestion in all earnestness, fortified by the fact that the same suggestion was advanced last year in the Marine and Fisheries Committee by the hon. member for Prince.

In regard to
the suggestion that the lbbster fishing season should start on the 5th August and end on 5th October I may say that Mr. Cowie, of the Marine Department, visited ou:r province last year and met the fishermen of the different sections of the coast at a number of duly advertised meetings. I presume Mr. Cowie also visited the New Brunswick shore and held similar meetings there. At those meetings fishermen came and submitted their evidence to Mr. Cowie. There is no doubt there has been a strong demand to have the season changed; but apparently last year there was not as strong a demand as in farmer years on account of the business of shipping live lobsters to the United iStates which has developed largely within the last few years. People concerned in that business felt that possibly the shipment of live lobsters in the early part of August, when the weather was extremely warm, would not be as beneficial and might not turn out as well as was desired. After ascertaining the opinion of a great many fishermen from the different localities along the coast the consensus of opinion seemed to be that possibly for this year it would be better for the season to commence at the same date, namely, loth August. The question of whether or not the lobsters were in a fit condition for human consumption at that time was also taken up, but there did not appear to be sufficient evidence to justify any definite conclusion. I am strongly of the opinion that the change suggested would be of great benefit to the fishermen because

it will enable them to save their lobster gear before the late storms make their appearance. I think the movement to open the season on August 5 would possibly meet with the approval of those interested. As I say the only possible objection was as to whether lobsters could be shipped ini proper condition in the hot weather.
While I am on my feet I should like to refer for a few minutes to the oyster industry in Prince Edward Island. I think those who have any practical knowledge of oysters will acknowledge that the Malpeque oyster, from Malpeque bay, Prince Edward Island, was the finest oyster ever put on the market. Perhaps I am not in order in discussing this question in connection with the present vote.
Go on.

A number of
years ago the local government, with the idea of developing ihe oyster industry, obtained control of the oyster areas from the Dominion government. The provincial authorities then leased those areas to people in the immediate vicinity of the beds, located in certain bays and rivers, and also accorded them !he privilege of importing American oysters for planting on those beds in the hope of stimulating production. As a result of the importation of these oysters some kind of disease or some species of insect was introduced and the consequence was that the areas which formerly produced oysters of such fine quality to such a wonderful extent were rendered completely non-productive, scarcely one live oyster being left in any of the bays or rivers. The report of a scientist who investigated the matter at the time showed that this destruction was the work of an insect which bored into the shell, or obtained entry into the body of the oyster in some way. However, the scientist in question was of opinion that after this devastation had run its course, which would probably occupy seven years, the insect would disappear, and restorative measures might be adopted. I have endeavoured to get some information on the subject from the Department of Marine and Fisheries but they do not seem to have any data which has any direct relation to it. I have also written to Dr. Knight on the subject but have received no reply as yet. The residents contiguous to the oyster areas, however, are of the opinion that the trouble has now disappeared and that the time is ripe for taking the steps necessary to re-stock the oyster beds. I think there has been some correspondence exchanged between the federal and provincial authorities with respect to the
latter transferring back the control of these oys'er areas to the Dominion government. It is impossible for the local government to undertake the work of developing and restocking the oyster beds because they do not possess the necessary funds. It is only through the instrumentality of the Department of Marine and Fisheries, therefore, that we can expect the necessary steps to be taken in the hope of restoring these devastated oyster beds to their former splendid condition. That such a work should be undertaken is most desirable. The oyster fisheries in the past constituted a great source of revenue to the fisherman of Prince Edward Island. When engaged in these fisheries he needed no expensive plant. For twenty-five or thirty dollars the fisherman could provide himself with a small boat and outfit, and his earnings from the oys'er fishery each fall would yield him from $200 to $300. Unfortunately the industry has been wiped out, and in consequence many people have been compelled to leave the province and seek employment elsewhere. As I have already said the Malpeque oyster was of unsurpassed quality. It was obtained from the unsullied waters of the Atlantic coast, uncontaminated by sewage from large cities as is the case of many of the oyster beds of the United States and elsewhere, and constituted a delicious food which in no way endangered public health. I do plead with the government to look into this matter and carry cut the necessary investigations with a view of seeing what can be done with a view of renewing these oyster beds and restoring them to their former healthy and productive state.

We have several
oyster beds in my constituency. Some of them are not doing well, but others are thriving. I doubt if the industry can really be made a success, but I hope the Department of Marine and Fisheries will investigate the matter fully and see what can be done in that direction. I understand the question of oyster development has been left to the different Maritime provinces for several years past, but that negotiations have been in progress with a view to transferring the oyster beds to the Federal government. I understand that two of the provinces have fallen into line and have decided to hand over the oyster beds to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, but Prince Edward Island has not yet followed the example set by those two provinces. I hope that province will do so soon, in order to allow the department to go into this matter with some degree of seriousness.

Oyster culture has been adopted by several countries of the world. China, for instance, has cultivated oysters for the last three hundred years. Japan and the United States have also gone into the business very extensively and have made a success of it, after spending large sums of money and having met with a great many failures. However, I believe the question is of sufficient importance to justify^ this government going into it in order to ascertain whether or not oyster culture can be made a success.
We have in my constituency the Caraquet oyster beds which are the most important in the Maritime provinces, perhaps with the exception of the Malpeque in quality and the Buctouche in quantity. The old world famed St. Simon oyster has met the same fate as the Malpeque oyster, being almost extinct, but, however, not completely so. Some years ago the fishermen in Caraquet gave up oyster fishing, because they could not get any oysters. But three years ago the fishermen found there were oysters on these beds and they went fishing, with the result that 500 barrels of oysters were marketed. Two years ago 800 barrels were fished and last year they increased their output to some 1,300 barrels, which goes to show that the Caraquet oyster bed would be very profitable. I should like to know if the Department of Marine and Fisheries has made any endeavours to induce Prince Edward Island to go into the industry, and if so what is the intention of the department with regard to the matter.
So far as the lobster season is concerned I doubt very much if our people are unanimous in regard to the open season. There is a great deal of inconvenience when one section of the coast has a spring season and the other section a fall season. If it were possible to give a fall season to the northern section of New Brunswick as well as the section south of Chockfish, and in the whole of Prince Edward Island, I believe it would simplify matters to a great extent, and would benefit the fishing industry. In my constituency fishermen have a season starting on the 26th April, and very often in the latter part of April and the early part of May the coast is still icebound in that section, and therefore the fishermen lose part of their season. Last year a great part of the season was lost on account of weather conditions. This year so far fishermen in Gloucester are doing well, but I doubt if they will favour changing the spring season for a fall season. All these matters should be the subject of very serious investigation and inquiry, and should not be dealt with without proper consideration. I think they should be very care-
fully gone into by the Department of Marine and Fisheries.

My hon. friend (Mr. Robichaud) must not take too much to heart my remarks about changing the lobster season. I never mentioned his part of the province. I mentioned that section south of Chockfish as far as Bale Verte.
I would like to have an answer to my question, and I will state the reason. The delegate who called on the minister in the month of February, 1924, although authorized by the great bulk of the fishermen of that section to present the case to the minister, went back to his constituency; whether he was chloroformed or not I do not know', but he never made a report to any one, publicly or otherwise. Again a resolution was adopted by the Marine and Fisheries committee unanimously, and whilst the fishermen in that section wanted to have the fishing season begin on the 6th day of August, and were laying their plans accordingly, yet the department could not accede to their request, and made no answer *Whatsoever. My hon. friend from Prince (Mr. MacLean) told us that Mr. Cowie of the Department of Marine and Fisheries visited his section. I am delighted to know that it was Mr. Cowie who went there, because while I was there I have yet to hear of any notification of Mr. Cowie's visit in the Maritime provinces-. He was expected, I believe, to interview the representatives and the people, so that they in turn could get in touch with those most directly interested and obtain information on the subj ect.	Whom he interviewed I know not,
but I have to assume that he held meetings in view of the fact that he held several meetings in -Prince Edv'ard Island; but if he came to the conclusion that the consensus of opinion of the fishermen in that section was unfavourable to the 6th August as the opening date of the season, he must have come in contact with the very few who were opposed to the change. I submit that if a vote were taken of the whole fishing population of -that section, you would find that very few dissented from the idea that if the fish were in proper condition to market-and I verily believe they are-they would vote to change the regulation,, so that their fishing would not be placed in jeopardy every year as it has been in years past..
While the remarks of my hon. friend from Prince and the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Robichaud) rather diverted discussion to the oyster question, I w'ould again ask the minister, has he seriously considered this

The position in which the
department was placed was rather a difficult one. The year before last a report was made by Dr. Knight, of the Biological Board, against any change in the present season; last year, after the committee on fisheries had adopted this resolution, an officer of the department was sent to carry on an investigation, and the report of this officer was against any change in the regulation in the fishing industry. The department fully realizes the importance of oyster culture, but unfortunately, on account of difficulties in regard to jurisdiction over the oyster areas, it has been unable prior to the present time, to reach any conclusion and to establish any good system of culture. We have been communicating with the provincial governments of New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island, asking those governments to hand over to the federal government the oyster areas, in order to enab'e the Department of Marine and Fisheries to rtart a programme of some kind for the development and betterment of this interesting industry. So far we have been unable to secure the property or the right of going over all those areas. We have already reached certain conclusions with the provincial governments, but nothing as yet has been definitely settled. I hope, in the course of a very few weeks, I shall be in a position to state that an understanding has been reached between the federal and provincial governments. As soon as this understanding is arrived at, the department will be ready to endeavour to develop this very important industry of oyster culture.

Item agreed to.
Fish culture, $370,000.

This is quite a
large amount and, perhaps, it is the most important item in this vote. I should like to draw the attention of the committee to certain facts in connection with fish culture. Fish hatching and fish culture have been going on mow for some fifty years, and during that period we should know something as to the results. Unfortunately, it has been only very lately that any attempt has been made to find out where we stand and what we are obtaining by the expenditure of this large amount. There is what is known as the Biological Board which is assisting the department in this connection, and it has been studying the question. I should like to draw the attention of the committee to what I have personally observed. As a boy, I remember cans and cans of fingerlings being put into the lake where I fished when I was a boy and where I have lived for some years, and I have not seen one of those fish fully grown caught in that lake. That is an observation that should compel the attention of the committee. There are no doubt some abuses in connection with fish culture especially as regards the deposits 	' j
of the fry and fingerlings. We have been playing the political game too much, members being anxious to report to their constituents that they had been successful in having ten, twenty or thirty thousand fry or fingerlings deposited in this or that lake, without ever considering what the cost and results have been. Certain results have been obtained by the Biological Board who have had specially qualified officials studying the question, and while no doubt the minister is familiar with the facts they should I think be brought to the attention of the committee. In June, 1923, there were deposited in what is known as Gunstone brook near Aylmer, Ontario, some 5,000 fry, and in September, the official who was looking into the subject was able to take out alive from that part of the brook only 175. The question naturally arises as what happened to the others. The official came to the conclusion that he would take out of the stream all the enemy fish and after he had removed some 36 rock bass he obtained 41 fry in their stomachs. This would indicate the reason for the disappearance of the fry. Near the same stream, in what was know as Buck brook, there were also deposited
5,000	fry, and from that brook there were obtained some 1,500. What accounted for the difference between this stream and the other? The difference between the number of fry secured was due to the fact that before the fry and fingerling had been deposited in Buck brook a large number of enemy fish had been taken out. In 1921 there were deposited in Kelly's brook, Prince Edward Island, in the month of May, 10,000 trout, and in September by seining 3,000 were obtained. At the same time there were deposited in that stream 11,662 fingerling, and in September not one could be obtained. The result in this case was due to a different cause from that which prevailed in the other eases; in this instance there was not sufficient food in the brook to feed the fry and fingerling deposited there. A more remarkable demonstration was carried out in Kettle brook in Elgin county. In June, 1921, 10,000 fry were deposited, and in June, 1923, 101,000 were deposited. In that case trout a year and two years old should have been obtained, and yet after seining not one trout was got. Instead there were a number of suckers, minnows, rock bass, black bass, shiners, and other fish of that sort to the total of 159. This will indicate what happened to the fry at that point.
I think I have given some facts that should cause us to insist upon the department taking some action in this matter. We have gone on for fifty years spending this amount of , money on this work, and we have results

Supply-Marine and Fisheries
such as I have indicated. I am not going to say that the culture is absolutely useless in all cases; I have been shown where it has been Successful. Nevertheless I think that our fish culture in these brooks has been a waste of money, and this 'because we have failed to put into practice the recommendations of the Biological Board. Two things should be taken into consideration before we go on depositing fingerlings and fry throughout the country. There should be a study of the lakes in Which they are deposited to ascertain whether there is sufficient food to take care of them; and in the second place we should remove all enemy fish which are likely to destroy the fry and fingerlings.
This subject is closely connected with a matter that has been referred to many times in this House; I mean our tourist traffic. We have throughout Canada some of tihe most beautiful lakes that are to be seen anywhere, and altogether the conditions are ideal for the promotion of an extensive tourist traffic. Good fishing is an unfailing attraction, and we have now been for fifty years endeavouring to increase the number of fish in our lakes and streams both for sport and commercial purposes, with varying fortune. The time has come when we should take the question more seriously into consideration and deal with it in a businesslike way. It is unfortunate, I think, that this matter should be dealt with between the provinces and the Dominion without any real co-oiperation; there seems to be no responsibility, and we are going on in a slip-shod, blind, haphazard way in the work we are doing. It would be well for the department, acting in conjunction with the provincial authorities, to select some lakes such as Muskoka lakes and bodies of water to be found in Frontenac county, for instance, and on the advice of the Biological Board as well as that of practical fishermen in these districts, empty these lakes of all destructive fish before depositing any fry and fingerling. In that way only can any satisfactory results be secured from fish culture. The reports of the Biological Board are extremely interesting and instructive, but unfortunately . their recommendations have not so far been taken seriously by either the provincial or the federal departments. In the interests of our own people, and with a view to increasing the fish in our lakes and streams, looking to the development of a tourist traffic, I would suggest that this matter be seriously taken up by the department and that the Biological Board be set to work to devise some means of coping with the matter. And in my opinion only the
advice of that board should be followed as to where fry and fingerlings should be deposited.

My hon. friend has expressed the views of one of the members of the board. The resolutions' which have been adopted by the Biological Board have been agreed to and acted upon by the Department of Marine and Fisheries, and we have been advised by the board that in the meantime the existing hatcheries be maintained so far as, in the opinion of the department, this may be justified. We are following the recommendations which have been made by the Biological Board. We have asked them to appoint certain officers to carry on the investigation along the lines of their suggestion. The work will be undertaken this year. In these scientific matters we have to rely upon our experts, in other words, the Biological Board. We have never up to the present time refused to follow their advice.

I quite realize that it is a scientific matter, but I would draw the minister's attention to the fact that the officials of departments are still continuing in the old way. I know of cases inhere men have asked that certain lakes be cleaned out before the fry is put in them, but nothing has been done. In a word, the practical results that we might expect from this work are not being obtained.

No doubt the members
of the Biological Board are familiar with the characteristics of lobsters, but when they undertook to see if our Atlantic lobsters would flourish in the Pacific, they sent the lobsters westward and failed to take the plugs off their claws before dropping the lobsters into the sea, thus leaving them helpless. If that is the sort of thing they do we are better without the Biological Board. I understand that in Ontario the hatcheries for sporting fish are under the control of the provincial government, but that the hatcheries for the propagation of commercial fish are stiill under the control of the federal authorities. I know that in Nova Scotia the hatcheries have been a success. There is a hatchery three miles from Windsor where they propagate salmon and
5 p.m. trout, and its work has resulted in many of our streams being replenished with fish. For instance, the Avon river in days gone by was a good salmon stream, but for many years it was necessary to put absolutely restrictive regulations into effect in an effort to restock the river, and it was not until the hatchery was established that any improvement was effected. To-day

Supply-Marine and Fisheries
that is a very good salmon stream again. I do not know very much about the results obtained in connection with the Margaree and Bedford hatcheries, but I know that any interference with the hatchery system would not meet with the universal approval of our people in Nova Scotia. Probably we have advanced too quickly, but I submit to the minister that in so far as the artificial propagation of salmon and trout for the replenishment of barren streams is concerned, the hatchery sys'.em should be retained.
Far be it from me to criticize scientific men, but my experience of these scientists while I was in the Department of Marine and Fisheries was that they were, to say the least, not at all practical. For example, they would make recommendations to the department for the expenditure of vast sums of money before 'heir experiments had been really successful. Our fisheries are entitled to the greatest consideration, and I do not believe that the department is doing one-tenth for the industry that it should. However, this is a day of economy. I believe, though, that much of the money now spent for other things might more properly be devoted to encouraging the fishing industry of Canada. In Nova Scotia they that go down to the sea in ships follow a very hazardous calling. As my hon. friend from Kent (Mr. Doucet) said, when discussing the lohster fisheries, in the early spring the men put out many hundred dollars worth of fishing gear, and probably before they get one night's catch it is all destroyed by a gale suddenly springing up. So when these men ask for assistance that they may be able to make a decent living, I think the department should always lend them an attentive ear. Do not be inclined too much to take the advice of so-called biologists. If the Biological Board had their way they would always have some scientific reason why the fish should still1 be permitted to swim in the water . and the fishermen prohibited from catching them. The fewest restrictions possible should be placed upon our men who are engaged in fishing, for it is a hard calling. Every experiment which will have for its object the betterment of the fishing industry should be carried on, but biological experiments should not be indulged in to such an extreme as to spend a great deal of money on something that is not shown to be feasible. My experience of the department is that it contains many excellent officials who give their time wi'hout stint in an endeavour to evolve means for the betterment of the fishing industry. In all the departments I know you 
will find conscientious men, but in no de-par, ment can more conscientious men be found than in the Department of Marine and Fisheries. They are not all experts; no man can be an expert in all lines, but the men in that department with very few exceptions are endeavouring to do their best for this great national industry of Canada. I have no more to say than this: Keep up your hatcheries, at least for the purpose of replenishing barren streams, and do not pay too much atten'ion to your Biological Board until they can show that their scientific ideas are capable of being made feasible.

tlhat has been dome on that lake in hatching for the first time on the North American oontinent the spawn of the sturgeon. I would like to remind the minister of the advisability of an official in the Maritime provinces to study the question of the quahaug, otherwise known as the hard-shelled clam. The quahaug fishery was a valuable industry in that part of the country many years ago, so much so that the department feared for its depletion and shortened the fishing season. As a matter of fact, I think the season now is about a month or five weeks each year, and that is at a time when the local people are otherwise busily engaged and do not give very much time to that industry. Unless those beds are raked regularly the fish will not thrive, and as a result the quahaug to-day is a very large size and is regarded by some as hardly suitable for marketing. I fear, and the majority of the people there fear, that unless some stimulus is given to that industry by lengthening the open season, possibly to the same length as the open season for oyster fishing, the quality of the fish will greatly deteriorate.
