Besides this there will have to be a renewal of flooring and other repairs of this nature. The work will be done by day labour.

Item agreed to.
Riviere aux Vases-wharf repairs and shed, $1,420.
Sir HENRY'DRAYTON:	What business
goes over this wharf?
The traffic at this point consists of cattle and freight and there are four steaonens that call at regular intervals with a capacity of sixty passengers. A population of about 1,600 is served.

Item agreed to.
Riviere du Loup (en bas)-wharf repairs, $4,900

The minister would not
allow this work to go without repairs, but why so much?

Item agreed to.
Riviere Ouelle-wharf repairs, $5,450.
This is a new item.

This vote is to
renew 40,000 feet board measure of flooring along the approach, 8,000 feet of sheathing on the headfolock, and to repair the concrete sheathing of the headblock.
Is this to be done by contract?
No.
Why not?

The engineers
report that it would be more economical to have the work done by day labour.
How many cubic feet of concrete will be used?

I have not the
estimate with me.
What riding is it in?
Kamouraska.
We do not know how much work is to be done.
The greater expenditure will be devoted to renewing the flooring and sheathing the headlock.

Work of this description
could easily be tendered for.

Has the engineer given
reasons why there should be no tender when the amount is over $5,000? If tenders are not to be called for you may as well
change the law.

All the material
going into the work is tendered for; but repair work of this kind, it has been shown, can be done better by day labour.

Had you not better
change the law instead of going on breaking it?
There is discretion under the law.

Item agreed to.
Roberval-wharf repairs and improvements, $13,850.

This vote is to
complete the contract with Messrs. Methot and Fournier for wharf improvements, amounting to $12,000, and to repair the shed flooring and sheating of the headlock at a cost of $1,650.

What member landed
this plum?

This is in the
county of Chicoutimi-Saguenay.

Item agreed to.

Supply-Harbours and Rivers
Ste. Adelaide de Pabos-wharf repairs, $1,200.

This is new. What
happened to the wharf?

This vote is to
repair the flooring and renew the stringers for a length of three hundred feet. The engineer reports that the repairs are essential for the maintenance of the wharf.
What riding is it in?
Gaspe. It is on the north shore of the St. Lawrence near Chandler.

Is that east or
west of Tadoussac and Murray Bay?
East.

How many people are
within a range of twenty miles, say, of this wharf?

I am told that
it is a very prosperous parish located four miles east of Chandler, in the county of Gaspe, with a population of about 2,350, engaged mostly in farming and fishing.

I understood
the minister to say that this was on the north shore.
It is on the south shore I find.

I was going to say we are now carrying on at great expense to the country a railway which skirts the whole of the north shore down to Murray Bay, and a great deal of the traffic is now looked after by the railway; therefore the same necessity for wharves there no longer exists.

Is the minister keeping
up all the wharves on the north shore too. I would not think there would be much business for them.

I do not think
many have been abandoned. Where you have a fishing population dependent on these wharves you will always have more or less water-borne traffic.

We made a
mistake in building the railway; it was to do the business.

It was not built
to serve those localities.

Item agreed to.
Ste. Anne de la Pocatiere-wharf repairs, $1,200.
Where is this place?

In Kamouraska
county.

Kamouraska county has
been very lucky. What is the reason?

This vote is to
renew the flooring and coping.
That is St. Alexis?

No, Ste. Anne
de la Pocatiere. St. Alexis was passed.

I do not know how it
passed. I did not hear it go.

We will go back
to St. Alexis if my right hon. friend wishes.

Item agreed to.
At six o'clock the Speaker resumed the chair and the House took recess.
After Recess
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

subtopic: THE LONDON MUTUAL FIRE INSURANCE COMPANY OF CANADA

speechtext:
Mr. W. X. BOYS (South Simcoe) (for Mr. Hocken) moved the second reading of and concurrence in amendments made by the Senate to Bill No. 10, respecting the London Mutual Fire Insurance Company of Canada, and to change its name to "London Fire Insurance Company of Canada."
Motion agreed to; amendments read the second time and concurred in.

Mr. FRANK S. CAHILL (Pontiac) (for Mr. Jacobs) moved the second reading of and concurrence in an amendment made by the Senate to Bill No. 14, respecting a patent of Edgeworth Greene.
Motion agreed to; amendment read the second time and concurred in.
Bill No. 164, for the relief of Walter Thomas Pratchett.-Mr. Church.

The House in committee of Supply, Mr. Gordon in the chair.
Harbours and rivers-Quebec-St. Antoine de Tilly- wharf reconstruction. $20,000.
Supply-Harbours and Rivers

Would the minister explain
this item?

This is required
for the demolishing of the existing head 'block, which is 49 feet by 39 feet, and the construction of a new head block 100 feet long by 40 feet wide. The engineer reports:
The present head block is all rotten and decayed, and in order to give necessary accommodation to navigation the construction of a new head block is imperative. There is no railroad in the locality, and the only means of communication and transportation are by navigation.
There are a number of parishes dependent upon this structure for accommodation, with a population of about 4,500.

Item agreed to.
St. Antoine de Tilly-dredging, $15,000.
This is to provide for a contract with the National Dock and Dredging Company for the execution of dredging at St. Antoine de Tilly, to dredge a channel 900 feet by 50 feet, to a depth of 6 feet.
Is this the same as last year?
Yes, an order in council was passed on the 17th of September of last year authorizing this contract.

Item agreed to.
St. Laurent d'Orleans-wharf repairs, $12,800.
What is this for?

This is to paint
the shed and hoisting apparatus, and repair the damage done to the approach which was washed out on a length of 160 feet. The new construction will consist of concrete walls on each side of the approach 179 feet long, with filling between, and concrete pavement. This wharf is a very old one, having been built in 1865. The engineer reports:
These repairs are required for the maintenance of the structure in good condition. The traffic is relatively heavy some 40 to 60 passengers being carried daily, both ways, by the S.S. Champion plying between Quebec, the island, St. Michel etc., and calling at St. Laurent twice daily during the summer season. On Sundays the traffic is increased to 200 or 300 passengers each way. This steamer carries also a few tons of freight daily. Some schooners call occasionally, and one of them regularly each week. The wharf is also a good shelter for the small navigation and the proposed expenditure will be of a public nature.

I understood the minister to
say the repairs weTe due to the washing away of the -wharf. What was it constructed of? If it was constructed of cement I do not see how it would wash away.
IMr. CahilU

My hon. friend
apparently does not understand. The new construction will consist of concrete walls. The old wharf apparently was constructed on the bank of the river, and the timber of which it was built has been washed away. That happens very often.

That is what I wanted to
know. The former wharf was of wooden construction?

Yes, and it is
to be reconstructed of cement.

Item agreed to.
Ste. Petronille (island of Oril earns)-wharf repairs and improvements, $5,000.
This is another very substantial item.

This is to repair the damage done in the fall of 1924 to the wharf expropriated in 1923-24, by replacing the stone filling washed away, and to repair the flooring of the slip, construct a new floating pontoon, and to enlarge the approach by means of a triangular-shaped addition 175 feet along its outer face composed of a concrete wall with stone filling.

How much was spent
on this work last year?
We spent $14,463 last year.

Will this further vote
complete the work?
This will complete the work.

Why is there no revote in
regard to this work if only $14,000 were spent last year?	[DOT]

Apparently there
was damage done to the wharf last year, the stone filling being washed away.

But why was there not a
revote this year when $37,100 was voted last' year?

We expected to
clean it up last year.
I thought you said that only $14,000 was spent?

The remaining
vote lapsed.

If $37,100 was voted
last year and only $14,000 was spent then the minister would be before us for a revote for the balance.

Supply-Harbours and Rivers
We are mot asking for it.

That is the explanation
the minister has always given of what revotes are.

At the time our
estimates were made up we expected to complete the work.

That is all right, but
the minister did not complete it; he only spent $14,000.
Yes.

How is it the balance
does not appear as a revote?

It might appear
as a revote but we did not know at the time our estimates were made up that there would be any balance. We expected to complete the structure.
At the time the estimates were made up?

Yes. I have already explained the nature of the work proposed to be done. Probably I should also explain that the department took over this wharf last year, and an award wias made by the Exchequer court to the amount of $29,604.45.
To whom was that award made?

The owner of
the- wharf.

It is a private wharf
then?

It was, but not
now; it was taken over last year.

I notice that when this item
first appeared-apparently in 1923-24-the sum of $37,100 was voted. The same amount appeared in 1924-25. This year the vote asked for is $15,000. Was the contract price originally $37,100?
No.

Then where do these figures
come in?

That was the
original estimate for the purchase of the wharf. Judgment was rendered by the Exchequer court awarding $29,604.45, and this is to complete the repairs that were undertaken last year.

When was the award made
by the Exchequer court?

Judgment was
rendered by Mr. Justice Audette on May 23, 1924, fixing the amount of the compensation at $29,604.45 with interest at 5 per cent to November 20, 1923. An appeal has been taken to the Supreme Court of Canada from this judgment.

I could understand the estimate appearing for that year for the amount of the wharf, but apparently before the award was made-I judge before the matter was positively determined; it is pretty hard to say from the information given-an item of $37,100 appeared in the estimates. That is what I cannot understand. I should not have thought the minister would know what he had to pay until the award was made. Then he would ask the House for an estimate for that amount and that amount exactly, whereas he is asking here for $37,100.
We had not only to expropriate and pay for the wharf, but we had repairs to make. We spent $14,463 last year in repairs.
When did the government decide to take this wharf over?

There	was an
estimate in 1923, for this wharf. We decided to acquire the structure, and the expropriation proceedings were carried on in May, 1924, and the award given.
That is to say there was an amount to acquire the wharf and an amount to improve it in the estimates for 1923-24?
Yes.

And at that time the
wharf belonged to somebody else?
Yes.
What damages would we be liable for if the wharf was a private wharf? What did the government do to the wharf to cause damages?

The government
required the wharf. This was a private wharf and a very important one.
Oh, it is the expropriation price?

The government
decided in 1923, they would purchase the wharf. They were not able to agree with the present owners and they went to the Exchequer court in 1924, and received the award of the court. There is nothing unusual in this procedure.

Supply-Harbours and Rivers

But the award was $29,-
000.

What were the reasons which
prompted' the department to acquire this wharf?

It is a very important wharf but the public were not getting the access to it that they should. The owners were not giving the public the opportunity they should get of using the wharf even by the payment of tolls; the wharf was blocked at times, and the gates were opened to suit the convenience of the owners. They *ere running a ferry service, and did not permit the easy access of other people who required the use of the wharf.
How many people live on the island?

I will give my
right hon. friend a statement of the traffic on the wharf, and it will give him an idea of the population. I have not the population at present. My note reads:
The traffic on this wharf is very important; La Cie Maritime de Levis operates the steamers Frontenac (304 gross tons), built in 1899, and Champion (482 gross tons, built in 1897). The former makes the service between Quebec, Lauzon and Ste. Petronille and the latter makes the service between Quebec, Ste. Petronille, St. Laurent, St. Jean, St. Michel and Berthier. During the summer season the Frontenac makes eight round trips daily and the Champion one daily trip during the week and two on Sundays. During spring and fall the number of trips is much less and during winter the S.S. Queen, belonging to another company but having the same managers, makes a few trips occasionally to Ste. Petronille. At Ste. Petronille during the summer season, the traffic consists of 200 to 300 people daily and 10 to 15 automobiles and other vehicles. On Sundays this number is increased to 1,500 to 2,000 passengers and 40 vehicles; general freight to about 15 tons weekly. All these quantities on the traffic are for the traffic from Quebec to Ste. Petronille, the same quantities are transported on the way back to Quebec.
The imports consist of general merchandise and provisions for a value of $70,000 and the exports consist of:
Fruits	 $ 75,000
Vegetables	 8,000
Fish	 io!ooo
Meat	and	poultry	 40,000
Hay	 1000
Total exports	 $134,000
Carried.
I am glad to know the hon. member for Sherbrooke has arrived. How many people live on the island of Orleans?

It is only an island.
There are six big parishes, and the upper part, called Ste. Petronille, just facing Quebec, is

a big summer resort. During the winter all the traffic is done over the bridge towards the (Sault Montmorency. During the summer from Ste. Petronille the traffic goes to St. Joseph de Levis, Lauzon and Quebec. There is heavy traffic going there. Most of the traffic passes through Ste. Petronille every morning. I think there are over 40,000 people on the island.
Permanent residents?
Yes, six big parishes on the island, 21 miles long, four miles from Quebec, and the upper part is a summer resort of great importance.

How many wharves on
the island?	-
I think there are four.

If there is so much
business done there, would it not have paid the private owners to have made a charge for the wharf? What I do not understand is the enxiety of the people there not to make any money if possible out of their industries.

The private
owners did make a charge, but I understand they had difficulty with the public who were not being accommodated, and there was great complaint.

Who were the private
owners?

La Cie Maritime
de Levis.
Perhaps if the hon. member for the riding would tell us it would be simpler.

I am not the member for the riding. It is in the constituency of the hon. member for Quebec County, (Mr. Lavigueur) but it is pretty near my riding. There is a ferry boat plying between Quebec, Lauzon and Ste. Petronille every two hours during the summer season, and) along in the fall all the traffic of the island is done through Ste. Petronille. The company is La 'Cie Maritime de Levis. They have two boats plying there.

That is the
company that owns the boats?
Yss.

The company
that does the business own this wharf. They have two boats and look after the whole accommodation. They did that, supplying their own wharf. Then we buy them out paying them $29,000, and we are now going to spend

Supply-Harbours and Rivers
a whole lot more in fixing up this wharf. How do they stand with us? What are we charging them?

They are not
operating.

The boats are
still running and it is still the same company.

Boats are running there
but I do not know to whom they belong.

Or did we buy
the boats at the same time? I think the $29,000 would be enough to include the boats as well.
Oh no.

Perhaps that
part of the bargain was overlooked. Is it not a fact that this wharf was owned by this company which looked after the traffic? While in the first instance, before we expropriated, the company had to look after this wharf, at least to the extent of being able to carry on business, we pay them $29,000 for the privilege of relieving them of that obligation, and we are not charging them anything now; or if we are charging them anything, how much?

This wharf is
probably the most important wharf on the island. It is in the proximity of Quebec city, and the representatives of the department thought that the public were not being served, and that this wharf should foe under the control of the government of Canada. The wharf was bought and is an important wharf, not only to the community of the island, but to those districts adjoining the city of Quebec, especially the city of Quebec, where many people who are residents of Quebec go back and forth to the island of Orleans.

Is it suggested that the owners of the wharf do not want to part with it? It is hard to understand why they should object. Previously they constructed the wharf and had to pay for the maintenance of it.

They do not
want to dispose of their wharf.

I cannot for the life of me
see why they would not, because the situation is that they are relieved of the repairs to the wharf in the future, they get $29,000 and the free use of the wharf in an improved condition, and the only answer given by the minister is that the public are being better served.
I cannot see why in the world the company desiring to do business would not be glad indeed to have both freight and passengers using the wharf. It seems to me the reason given by the minister is not a substantial one. It looks like a mighty good bargain for the company. Not only has the government paid them $29,000, but it seems to me they have paid the difference between $29,000 and the amount of this vote, the difference being repairs. Therefore, I cannot see how it can be argued for a moment that that is not a deal which ought to satisfy the owners.

The owners were not anxious to sell. Service was not being given to the public; we took over the wharf and as soon as the wharf is in a state of repair so that it can be handed over to the Marine department, a charge will be made by that department.

The charges made by
the Marine department are purely nominal.

They have not
been changed recently.

No, but the wharf was
not bought before. Nobody will dispute the fact that from the size the hon. member (Mr. Dedhene) gives for the island and the traffic that there is there, even if it is only holiday traffic, tourists, there Should be a good substantial wharf. But apparently there was one.

It was in a very
bad state of repair.

The minister made war
against the owner and declared that the government was going right in to take his wharf away from him. I know there must have been a few sad houre in the directorate of that company when it was made known that the minister was going unmercifully to take their wharf away from them. There would be weeping and gnashing of teeth in that directorate. This was a wharf which they had had for many years and which they had had to maintain in a state of repair, and the minister was wanting to take it away from them at a cost of $29,000. Therefore, they would not have a dollar of repairs; they would get the use of the wharf at a nominal price, or, perhaps, nothing-nothing up-to-date-and they would have the $29,000 in their pockets.

They wanted
sixty.

Certainly. Who would
not? If they knew the minister, they cer-

Supply-Harbours and Rivers
tainly would work hard for sixty. Why are we in an aggressive campaign reaching out to get all the wharves we can and to take them from private owners? Are there any wharves left in the country that the minister can still get his hands on? Surely we have enough responsibility putting wharves where they are needed without tearing after the ownership of men who are ready to keep them. No man in the world having a wharf would deny the public the use of it for a fee. How many more expropriations has the minister made in order to get more to do and more money to pay out?

There is not very much in my right hon. friend's criticism. This wharf is an important one to the people, not only of the island of Orleans, but to the city of. Quebec and the adjoining country. That is shown by the traffic and the people who go over it. The wharf is in a very bad state of repair. It was not serving the public. Representations had been made that we should take it over. You cannot say that one section of the people should have a public wharf and another section should not. My right hon. friend says that we are taking over wharves. I am glad to say that we are taking wharves on water. Heretofore, there have been wharves taken on dry land.

Is the hon. member
referring to the sawdust wharf?

No. One of
more recent date. If he washes to push that, I will tell it,
Tell us now.

What is this
horrible thing?

I do not like
that manner of criticism. My right hon. friend is familiar with the city of Quebec and the island of Orleans. He knows it is an island of great richness, great agricultural wealth.
I have said that.

It should be
properly served, and the taking over of this Wharf will serve a public interest there. The arrangements which the department has made are proper and fair and there should be no great criticism.

Does the department
intend that these wharves shall be self-sustaining?

The government
of Canada has never contended that, and when I say that, I say it of all governments.
To about what percentage wall it be self-sustaining?

Once the wharf
is in shape to be transferred to the Department of Marine and Fisheries, I have no doubt a fee will be charged to the steamers that go there.

That would not pay for
doing the morning sweeping.
I quite agree with my right hon. friend. I do not know why there should be so great a desire just now for a change of policy on the part of my right hon. friend.

I am complaining, not of a change of policy, but of the taking away into the government's possession of a wharf that was there already. The explanation given was that the man was not letting the public use it. That is no explanation because no man would act in that way unless he was anxious to lose all the money he could. If the wharf is there, it is in his interest to keep it in shape for service and to give the service. What I do not understand is the policy of expropriation.

The matter was
canvassed very carefully and it was considered to be in the public interest that the wharf should be taken over.

Who are the
directors of this company?

I have not the
information here.
One might learn more from that than from the name of the company.

This matter was
dealt with originally last year and the year before, I think. My notes are deficient tonight in regard to the ownership and the directorate.
What was the offer made by the department before expropriation proceedings became necessary?

I have not that
information in the notes of this year. I expect it will be somewhere in the neighbourhood of the award1. I know our estimate of value was very much below the valuation placed upon the wharf by the owner, and the matter was referred to the Exchequer court and a price arrived at.

Supply-Harbours and Rivers
What did the department consider to be the value, even if the minister had not the information as to t'he actual offer made?

I think we had
the full information last year when the matter was before parliament. I do not know whether it was discussed or not. The history has not been carried forward in our notes.

Was there no other place where a wharf could have been built? If the department had shown a marked desire to build another wharf at some other point, the owners would have been willing, perhaps, to give them the wharf for nothing.
I understand that the engineer's report was to the effect that this was the best place for a wharf.

The people who carry on this steamship service, before expropriation, would require a place at which to land their boats, to take their passengers on and put them off. They had this wharf and were maintaining it. They have been paid $29,000. The government have spent, or intend to spend, $23,100 in connection with repairs over and above the $29,000. At the present date the owners have the $29,000 in their pockets and they have the wharf service as before.

That is practically true except that there is an appeal to the Supreme court from the decision of the Exchequer court. As regards the expropriation of this wharf, it was not gone into lightly at all. The whole situation was thoroughly canvassed. They were not allowing the general public to use the wharf, and representations were made by the people there that they should have a public wharf at that point. I cannot see why these people should not have the same facilities as others.

I cannot reconcile the minister's statement that these people had a wharf and passenger boats with his assertion that they would not allow the public to use this wharf. That seems so repugnant to business principles that it requires some explanation.

I think I can give
the explanation. The macadamized roads on the island were completed by the provincial government only about two years ago and there are about forty miles of extremely good highways throughout the island, so that the motor traffic that has developed there during the last three years or so is simply tremendous. This wharf was owned by a private
company who of course were able to land passengers from their own boats, but no boats owned by anybody else could approach the wharf. There is an enormous traffic by schooners, motor launches and yachts that ply between this point and Quebec and the company were unwilling to have the passengers landed at this wharf. Furthermore, there were no facilities to accommodate the motor traffic, which is considerable. In view of all these facts therefore numerous petitions were forwarded to the government requesting that the wharf be purchased in the interests of the general public.

Does the hon. member suggest
that the people engaged in this varied traffic are really anxious to do 'business at this wharf?
Only the company's boats have been allowed to land passengers there.

The suggestion is that people
want to do business at the wharf and that the company will not allow them to do so. Would it not b'e a good idea for the government to build some other wharf? I understood the minister to say that they considered the amount awarded too high and did not offer anything like so much.

I did not say
that.

Did the Exchequer court
award something for the wharf and another sum for loss of trade sustained? Perhaps the minister has the judgment and can give us some idea of the findings of the court.

I said I had not
before me the amount offered but that apparently there was a great difference between the department and the owners and that the matter had gone to the Exchequor court. The court awarded a certain sum which the owners were not prepared to accept and I understood from my notes that they were appealing to the Supreme court. I think the main consideration is to convince the committee that this wharf is a public necessity and if I can do that then I do not think there should be any reason for not voting the item.

We were convinced of
that long ago.

Then there ought to be no further discussion of the matter. The people of the district were not properly served under the old conditions, and as a matter of fact the owners were allowing the

Supply-Harbours and Rivers
wharf to go into disrepair, as will be seen by the amount the government has spent. They were not giving to the general public the service that was needed and complaints were received from the island to this effect.
We should have the judgment of the court in this matter. I want to find out whether there was an award for loss of business as well as for the value of the wharf.

Does the hon. member
(Sir Eugene Fiset) know of any merchants in the district who refuse to sell their goods for cash? The explanation given by the hon. member for Rimouski-
Is true.

I was not referring to
its veracity at the moment; I was merely commenting on the marvel of the thing. I cannot understand why people would be there to do business and would refuse to do it.

The people could
not afford to buy other boats.

Perhaps they could not
run any more boats. But here they have a wharf, a money-making enterprise, and the minister tells us that the company allowed their own boats to use it but not the motor boats of other people, nor automobiles. Why would they not allow this traffic to use the wharf? It seems so foolish. Can the hon. member give an explanation as to why they would not?

These people were
using launches instead of the company's boats. That is a very simple explanation.

But could the company
not charge a fee for the use of the wharf? I can understand that they would not want to provide facilities for nothing.

A nominal fee of
five or ten cents would not pay them.

But they could fix a higher fee. I think the most obvious thing is that a lot of money has gone into the pockets of the company; and that is the chief difference between the condition now and that of three years ago. There is a big hole in our treasury and a fine wad in their bank account. Will the minister undertake to bring down, the next time his estimates are under consideration, a statement of the amount offered by the government together with a copy of the judgment of the court?
I will bring it down; I regret it is not here to-night. I had a statement in my notes on the negotiations leading up to the purchase.

Item agreed to.
St. Roch des Aulnaies-wharf repairs, $1,250.
This is a new item.
This is for the repair of a wharf in the L'Islet district.
Is this just ordinary decay?
This vote is to renew 5,000 feet of stringers and 7,000 feet of flooring and to provide 80 cubic yards of stone filling.	[DOT]

Item agreed to.
St. Ulric (riviere Blanche)-wharf repairs, $2,200.
Where is this?
This is in Ma-tane county.
This is not the celebrated Matane wharf?
No.
Has the minister decided that he has wasted enough money on the Matane wharf, or is there a vote for it somewhere?
It will come later.
The minister is waiting for the supplementary estimates. It is rather unfortunate that he cannot get hotter weather than this for the supplementary estimates.

Item agreed to.
Ste. Victoire-wharf repairs, $2,950.
Where is this?
This is in Richelieu.

What is the trouble
here?

The work will
consist of rebuilding from the low water level the stone-filled crib high level section of the wharf and renewing part of the stringers and the flooring of the lower section. All the timber and lumber of the high level wharf is gone and a complete reconstruction is urgently needed.

Item agreed to.

Supply-Harbours and Rivers
Sabrevois-wharf repairs, $1,100.
Where is this?

In 1924-25 we spent $8,885 and the exact amount the year before was $71,892. Last year there was a reconstruction of what is known as the Bureau wharf. As regards the shed, the other night I undertook to give certain information with reference to the revenues collected' at Chicoutimi. When the Chicoutimi basin item was under discussion on May 29, I gave two sets of revenue figures as follows: First, $145 for 1922 and $240 for 1923; second. $4,928 for 1921. $5,638 for 1922 and $7,818 for 1923. As these figures did not appear to agree, I promised to have them verified at a later date.
I may now say that the smaller figures represent harbour dues collected by the harbour master, in those years, from ships entering the harbour, while the larger amounts show the -revenue received by the wharfinger for goods -passing over the wharf. Both sets of figures are correct, one representing harbour dues and the other wharfage revenue. I think the question raised is worth investigating and we will have a return made showing the revenues collected from these various works.

The minister
might supplement that by showing the expenses, so that we may know what the net revenue is.

The net revenue
in some of these cases will not be so large.

But it is the
facts that we want.

At Chicoutimi
there has been a steady increase during the last two or three years and the net revenue would not be seriously affected.

materially affected. My hon. friend is not serious when he asks for all the expenses.

The net revenue over operating costs? The wharfinger of course would be paid a commission on the collections, which would be a comparatively small amount. I will see that the committee gets that information.

The Minister
of Marine (Mr. Cardin) has not told us how he is going to straighten out the tangle under his own act. I do not know whether it should be a question for the courts or for the Auditor General or for a bill of complaint, or what. But surely the matter should not be allowed to go on in this way.

The practice that is now being followed is not a new one. In the port of Montreal as well as at Vancouver and other ports under commissions, money has been spent by the Public Works department, and not later than last year parliament *approved of an item of $500,000 to be expended in the port of Quebec by the Department of Public Works, the amount having been voted in the estimates of that department. And this practice has been followed in many cases. I quite agree with my hon. friend that perhaps it might be more proper to have the money advanced to the harbour commission in the form of a loan as we are doing this year in the case of Quebec and as

we have done in the past for Vancouver. Possibly, I say, it might be better to proceed in that way; but the, practice of voting money through the Public Works department to be spent on harbours under the control of commissions is not a new one. It has been followed on other occasions.

First I will refer to an interjection which the Minister of Public W'orks (Mr. King. Kootenay) made in an undertone while his colleague was speaking; he did his best to get the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to say that the same practice had been followed in Toronto as well. But the Minister of Marine being wiser ignored the suggestion. The reason is perfectly obvious. As I pointed out a little time ago to my hon. friend, who does not pay much attention to these things, the conditions in Toronto are absolutely different^ inasmuch as the harbour works there are directly the property of the city.
Supported by the Dominion government.

The city puts up a great deal more money in connection with the harbour than does the Dominion government; and the harbour works there are not under such an act as this any more than the harbour of St. John comes under any similar act. The question has come up time and again whether St. John should not be under a regular act such as applies to Montreal and Quebec, but so far this has not been deemed advisable. Now, the Minister of Marine says he is following precedent in this matter. I should' like him to point out any instance in which this has been done in relation to harbours of this class. Has it been done in connection with the harbour of Vancouver, the harbour of Montreal or the harbour of Quebec prior to this government's coming into office? This would be one way in which the obligations of the Quebec Harbour Commissioners could be improperly kept down. And I am not saying that it was not done last year, although that does not make it any better; indeed, it makes the Quebec harbour situation so much worse than the statements brought down would show. With a friendly government they have the Department of Public Works spending for them half a million dollars, and if that is precedent it is precedent that we should forget as quickly as possible. If my hon. friend knows of any other instance of the kind we had better hear about them and have the

Supply-Harbours and Rivers
matter straightened1 out. If our accounts in connection with our harbours are wrong-a3 they will be if we are going to allow work to be done by the Public Works department without charging it to the harbour commissioners in their books-then there is no good having accounts at all; we might as well put an end to the whole thing. In other words, an account to be of any use must be accurate, and it is not accurate if the country, through other votes, makes additions to the property of the harbour commission without charging it to them. I submit, Mr. Chairman, there should be regularity in connection with this question. Under the act of two years ago, Three Rivers got a full government endorsa-tion and became exactly the same as Montreal, and therefore should be governed by the statute. The minister may have forgotten about the change. I hope he will have this put upon a proper business basis. I think he might also let us know to what extent the power of paying salaries and the like is being exercised under that act. In the meantime, as far as I am concerned, the town can be happy with the addition of the Bureau wharf.

My hon. friend
has explained that there is no uniformity in the matter. We all know there has not been uniformity. He says the city of Toronto is treated differently from the district of Three Rivers. It may be. But the harbour affairs of Toronto are administered by a harbour commission, and the city have an interest in the harbour development. In St. John there is no harbour commission, but the city has a very large interest in the harbour works, and the Public Works department* has been responsible for their construction. That is also true with respect to the harbour of Quebec where many of the works were constructed by the Public Works department and turned over to the harbour board free of interest. That is true of Montreal.
Is my hon. friend quite sure of that?
Yes; and it is true of Vancouver.

If that is correct, the statements made by his friends in connection with the Quebec vote are entirely wrong, because they distinctly said that the work had been done by the Public Works department and the interest was charged up to the commissioners, they being forced to take over the works. Can my hon. friend give us the truth?

What statements
is my hon. friend referring to?

To statements
made in this House.

I know it is true of works in Montreal, in Quebec and in Vancouver, where certain works built by the Department of Public Works were taken over. It may be that the Minister of Customs (Mr. Bureau) brought down a bill two years ago which incorporated a commission for administering the harbour of Three Rivers, but he did not ask parliament to vote any money for administration purposes, and no money has been voted, it being the intention that the Public Works department should carry on the construction. I think that is the proper procedure for the development in that port, for the activities of the harbour are not such as require administration by a commission handling a large expenditure.

I should like
to find out who is right, the minister or his supporters. I will give just one instance. A wharf was built by the Department of Public Works in Quebec. Now, according to the minister's statement to-night, the commissioners have the right of running that work without being charged interest on it. Is that right?
That is my understanding.

If that be right, I just want to point out, Mr. Chairman, how easy it is for this House to be entirely misled, because absolutely different statements were made. It was said that the pier had been charged up to the commission, although they did not want it, and they were being charged interest on the outlay.
Not that pier.

I wonder how
many more piers the minister built there. I am still speaking of the one place, Quebec. Was another pier built in Quebec? If so, let us have it.

The next item is No. 150.
Dauphin Beach-wharf, $6,600.

I am aware, Mr. Chairman, that item No. 150 has been called, but I regret that I may have to be away a day or so next week and I wondered if the minister would have any objection to giving me information now relating to item No. 155. I asked a question or two the other night of the minister, but he had not his notes with him, and he would oblige me very much if he would give me the information now. If he is going on with item No. 155 in the first three days of next week I regret to say I cannot be here.

I have not the dredging items here, but if I remember rightly my hon. friend asked regarding the appropriation or expenditure at Collingwood. I have gone into the matter, and it is the intention of the department to do, out of the general dredging vote for Ontario and Quebec, certain work in the harbour of Collingwood this year to the amount of about $20,000 odd, I think.
What about Belle River?
I have not the information on that but I shall be very glad to give it to my hon. friend at a later date.

Of course I realize that I
am out of order and that I am entirely in the hands of the minister. I appreciate What he has told me already and if he will consent to give me the further information-I presume he knows it now

whether anything is included in this item for Belle River. I should like to know what the amount is.

I understand that my hon. friend has already been advised through the Public Accounts committee that there will be a further expenditure this year As to the amount I have not that information at hand, but there will be some further dredging at Belle River this year.

As a matter of fact I do know that about $10,000 will be required to complete certain dredging that was undertaken, but that does not for a moment indicate that there will not be more spent. In fact, something I saw yesterday would indicate that there will be further expenditure for a turning basin, and so on. I do not want the information unless I can get it accurately. If I can get it accurately I should certainly like to have it.

I think my hon.
friend is getting information day by day and getting it accurately.

That may be true as far as
expenditure is concerned but not as regards estimates for future expenditure, and that is what I am asking for.
I will get the estimate.
Then I understand the minister is not in a position to give me definite information to-night.

There will be
further expenditure as I have already informed my hon. friend. As a matter of fact I understand the work is to be contracted for, and it would be only an estimate that I could give my hon. friend.
That is all I want.
What is the expenditure on Dauphin beach for?

This is a revote
of $6,600. It is required to provide for the construction of a wharf 464 feet 6 inches long over all, measured on the outside. The wharf will consist of a stone fill approach, 200 feet long, and 12 feet wide on top, with slopes of one and a half horizontal to one vertical, a pilework extension to this approach 152 feet long and 12 feet wide, and' an "ell," 112 feet 6 inches long and 12 feet wide, with triangular extension 20 feet from inner comer. The pilework section throughout will be close piled on the outside.

When was this wharf
started?	.

The work is under contract, an order in council having been passed on December 22,	1924, granting
authority for the acceptance of the tender of Isaac Silverwood, of Dauphin beach, Manitoba.

What is the total cost
of the work?

This vote will
complete the work. The .contract price is $5,990; and inspection, contingencies, and so on amount to $610.

Why was $8,800 voted
last year?

It was voted but we did not get our contract let until December. We only spent $659 last year. The amount voted last year was an estimate of the cost. When tenders were called for we found that they varied from $5,990 to $8,962.

The work is going on

Yes.
This is surely a summer resort is it not?

No. The district is a dairy farming country, settled by Canadian, English and Ruthenian settlers, and there are a great many returned soldiers settled there. There are two creameries in the town of Dauphin, and they are handling a very large volume of cream. In addition to dairying there is some truck farming and cattle raising.

I hope the minister will
excuse me smiling. The Dauphin country is a splendid farming country, one of t.he best in the province, but Dauphin Beach is a summer resort.

My right hon.
friend has local knowledge and so can enlighten the committee. I regret that I have not any such knowledge.

I presume this vote is
the result of government policy, and I am not at the moment criticizing it; what I should like to do is to get the facts. The minister has said that there is some dairying and cattle raising, and that there are Canadian, English and Ruthenian settlers; but the nature of the farming country at Dauphin has no more relation to the requirements of the wharf at Dauphin Beach than the depth of snow at the pole has to do with it, not a particle. Dauphin Beach is a summer resort, on lake Dauphin about a dozen miles or so to the east of *Dauphin. If it is used for any other purpose I should like to know what it is. I would not think that very many Cunard or White Star liners get into lake Dauphin.
I would not expect it. Still there are a number of people there who do use the lake.
But only for fun.

They have no
railway connection. They must depend upon the lake to transport their products to market, and Dauphin is their only market. My information is there is considerable farming population that use this lake during the summer.
I know there is.

In addition to
that it is used by the people who go there to enjoy the beach and the boating.

That is what I wanted
to know.

The hon. member for
Dauphin (Mr. Ward) is not here. But I have been in constant communication with him, and I understand there is a very considerable traffic across the lake, by those who bring their produce to market. I am not very familiar with the district myself but that is what I understand from the hon. member in whose constituency it is.

Does the Minister intend
that any of this appropriation shall be used to repair the dykes on the Assiniboine river? Some of them were washed out during the flood this spring. The minister gave figures

Supply-Harbours and Rivers
a moment ago stating that $4,000 odd were spent in the year 1922, to repair dykes the government have had to build1 and maintain from year to year during the last forty years. I think in the neighbourhood of $50,000 has been spent by the federal government in building and keeping in repair dykes on the Assiniboine river between Portage la Prairie and Winnipeg. In 1922 they undertook to repair .the dykes which were damaged by the flood of that year. We had a flood again this spring and I am informed that some damage has been done, the extent of which I do not know. I have received a communication from the municipality of Cartier asking me to use my influence with the government to have them give a grant to that municipality of $5,000; and stating that if they get this grant the municipality will undertake to repair the dykes themselves. If these dykes are not repaired this year it may spell disaster to a good many farmers situated along the banks of the river next summer.

Minor repairs
might be made to works previously constructed by the Dominion government, but I can assure my hon. friend that . the government has no intention of undertaking any large dyking scheme along the Assiniboine river.

I understood the minister
to say the government would be willing to repair dykes previously constructed by the government.

We will be advised by our engineers as to what work we will do this year, but it is not the intention of the department to make the government liable for large undertakings on the Assiniboine river.

I know that perfectly well, but I should like to get an assurance from the minister that the department will undertake to repair the dykes which they previously constructed. It will be a very small item. Surely he can give me such an assurance, because otherwise those people will be knocking at the door of the government this summer or next fall asking them to puit those dykes in shape before the freshet occurs next spring. I think it is reasonable to ask for an assurance now that the work will be undertaken. It may only cost a few hundred dollars, but of course I am not in a position to say definitely. Two years ago it cost $4,000 odd. Will the government spend that much money on those dykes if necessary?

If the hon. member will tell me the district he has in mind I will have the matter investigated and ascertain what is involved and the liability of the Dominion government. I will then answer his question.

Yes, that is sufficient. I
will be .glad to furnish the information to the minister. I understand that following up a delegation that was introduced to the minister in the year 1922, the department agreed to make a survey of that portion of the Assiniboine river lying between Portage la Prairie and Winnipeg, to see if something could not be done to keep the waters of the Assiniboine river within their boundaries and thus prevent the flooding of the agricultural lands adjacent to the river. I understand the department undertook that survey and that it has been completed.

Yes, we made
the survey.
What is the estimate?

A large estimate,
amounting to some hundreds of thousands of dollars, made by our engineers, has been forwarded to the provincial departments of public works, who have been making certain investigations, and correspondence has taken place between ithe provincial departments of public works and the department at Ottawa.
What is the provincial estimate?
I could not say. It has only recently been referred to them. It is very much less than our estimate.

Yes, that is right.

There is considerable discrepancy there. I am well acquainted with the situation out there, and I would hesitate to advise the government to undertake any expenditure involving a million dollars in that district. I believe that with a proper supervision over the river when it is in flood a good deal of the damage could be taken care of, and there would not be the damage that has frequently occurred. The trouble has been that the provincial engineers have passed the buck to the federal engineers and the federal engineers have said, "The responsibility is not ours; it rests with the municipalities and the provincial government". An ice jam occurs on the river and nobody has any authority to immediately break up that ice jam, and t'he result is that the water overflows and floods the surrounding land. I believe that if there were proper supervision of the floods in the spring, and if the ice jams were broken up before they had seriously formed it would immediately relieve the situation and the water would flow away. I know that when the engineers got busy at Portage la Prairie this spring they undertook to break up the ice jams as soon as they formed and prevented serious floods. It seems to me with the equipment we 'have now, with the modern airships, supervision could be undertaken from the air. Bombs could be dropped from the air and these ice jams could be broken up and the situation relieved before they become dangerous.
It would be something like a war.

It would be good practice for us in case of future war. One feature of this is that the place where the ice jams form is where the river takes a turn, where there is a bend, in the river; that is where the jam forms and that is the dangerous point that should be watched. That is another phase of it that would not cost very much money. You could dig channels across the necks of land where the river takes a turn, and if that were done, in a few years these channels would become the course of the river. In that way you would hasten the flow of the water down to the Red river at Winnipeg. The water would run away more quickly at the mouth and I do not think it would be a serious menace to the city of Winnipeg. If you cut off the narrow necks of land and put engineers in there who would break up the ice jams when they occurred, with the expenditure of not very many thousand dollars you could take care of the

situation and relieve the pressure at Portage la Prairie, always bearing in mind that the dykes constructed now are along the little runways and creeks and must be maintained in proper shape.

I am a little disappointed, after listening to the speech of the hon. member for Portage la Prairie. I thought he would put in a word for some places west of Portage la Prairie on the Assiniboine river. We have lots of floods through the Brandon constituency. If a dyke is to built I hope the minister will not forget that district.
You want a bombing machine there.

I am sorry I was not in the House when the appropriation for wharves was going through, because I notice from the Canada Year Book we export more fish from Manitoba than they do from New Brunswick, and the idea that we can get off with a $6,000 vote for wharves astounds me altogether when so much business is being done. The item however, is passed and we cannot get anything out of it now.

The Netley cut is an artificial waterway dredged by the department in 1014, between the Red river and Netley lake. What was the idea of the cut?

It was suggested to permit of Netley lake being entered by small boats and flat-bottomed scows. It was represented that there was a considerable quantity of cordwood and hay on the shores of and adjacent to Netley lake, and that settlers and others interested experienced difficulty in having it taken out.
What did the minister say had happened since then?

It was found that it was not serving the purpose for which it was constructed, and that it was impossible to maintain a bridgeway or roadway over the cut. It is considered cheaper to close the cut than to try to maintain a bridge at that point. I have not the original cost of construction.

The construction in the first place is one example of the unnecessary expenditure of public money. It connects the Red river with Netley lake which lies to the west of the Red river. The excuse given to the department for the construction of this channel was that a quantity of hay and cord-wood could be shipped through it on scows. Netley lake is very shallow and there are no wharves around it. My information was that no scow ever went in there and that nothing was ever shipped through the channel. I am informed that that was not the real purpose of its construction at all. There were one or two individuals in Selkirk who owned motor launches and who had a hunting lodge on Netley lake. They wanted a short cut to get in there in order to shoot ducks. That is the reason why this channel was constructed. After it had stood there for a few years, it began to fill up the channel of the Red river, because the water commenced to eat away the approaches on both sides. The soil is very marshy and the silt carried through the channel became a menace to navigation on the Red river. Therefore, the department began to fill it up. The filling up has been going on for some years, and the action of the river is so strong that they found it almost impossible to fill it up. I am afraid this vote will not complete the work. I thought it proper to bring this matter to the attention of the committee, because in the estimates that are brought before us each year there might be some other items similar to this.
No.
It was unnecessary in the first place, and I hope this item will finish the work of closing it up.

The contractors have asked to be compensated for the additional width of trench excavation and back fill rendered necessary. The district engineer has recommended this, and, as I say, I intimated to the committee last year that probably an item would be brought down in the supplementary estimates. Is this something we

formerly owned by a timber company that is not operating to-day. The dam is a distinct aid to navigation, and we propose to put it in repair.

Mr. Chairman, this vote represents a very important work. Late last fail the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Knox) and myself visited Cowan lake, which is the opening of navigation to the north country. Practically all the transportation of northern Saskatchewan is by the rivers and lakes. We found that since the Big River Lumber Company gave up their plant at Big river this dam has been neglected, and unless some improvements and repairs are made to it the navigability of Cowan lake and the rivers running north will be very largely diminished. We found scows were going to the north country taking supplies to the Hudson's Bay Company and to trapping posts, but they were only half loaded because the dilapidated condition of this dam seriously affected the navigability of Cowan lake and the rivers running north.
